paras: One cold winter morning, Emperor Akbar and Birbal were walking beside a lake. Akbar dipped his finger into the icy water and quickly pulled it out. “Nobody could stand in this water for a whole night,” he said.
“A person will do almost anything for money, Your Majesty,” replied Birbal.

So Akbar announced a reward: a thousand gold coins for anyone who could stand in the lake all night long. A poor washerman took up the challenge. Through the bitter cold night he stood in the water, shivering, and in the morning he came to the court to claim his prize.
“How did you survive the cold?” asked Akbar.
“Your Majesty, a lamp was burning far away in the palace. I kept my eyes on it all night, and it gave me strength.”
“Then you were warmed by the palace lamp!” said the emperor. “That is cheating. You get no reward.” The poor man went away heartbroken.

The next day Birbal did not come to court. Akbar sent a messenger, who returned saying, “Birbal says he will come as soon as his khichdi is cooked.” Hours passed, and still Birbal did not come. At last the emperor went to Birbal's house himself.
There he found Birbal sitting beside a small fire. High above it, tied to the top of a tall bamboo pole, hung a pot of khichdi.
“Birbal, have you lost your mind?” laughed Akbar. “How can the khichdi cook when the pot is so far from the fire?”
“In the same way, Your Majesty,” said Birbal politely, “that a man standing in a freezing lake was warmed by a lamp burning far away in the palace.”
Akbar understood his mistake at once. He called back the washerman, gave him his thousand gold coins, and praised Birbal for his wisdom.
Moral: Be fair, and never deny people what they have honestly earned.
